prompt: The number of older people is increasing. Some people think this is causing problems in their countries while others feel that older people play an important role in society. Discuss both views and give your opinion
essay:
A growing proportion of the population in many countries is now elderly, a demographic shift that has generated considerable debate. While some argue that older people make an invaluable contribution to society through their experience and expertise, others contend that an ageing population places a substantial burden on governments. Although the elderly can provide significant social and professional benefits, I believe that the financial and institutional pressures associated with population ageing are ultimately more consequential.

On the one hand, older people can make an important contribution to society because they possess knowledge and experience that cannot easily be acquired through formal education. In many professions, senior employees play a crucial role in mentoring younger colleagues, passing on practical expertise and helping them develop sound professional judgement. Beyond the workplace, older generations can also contribute to their communities through volunteering, childcare and other forms of social participation. Their experience and maturity can therefore strengthen both professional institutions and society more broadly. Nevertheless, technological developments have made it increasingly possible to preserve and disseminate knowledge through digital training programmes, online courses and recorded tutorials. As a result, some of the functions traditionally performed by experienced workers can now be replicated or supplemented by technology.

On the other hand, an ageing population can create significant economic and social pressures, particularly when the number of retirees rises relative to the working-age population. Older people are generally more likely to require healthcare and long-term social care, both of which can be extremely expensive to provide. Governments must also finance pensions and other retirement benefits, while a shrinking workforce may result in a smaller tax base with which to fund these services. Consequently, public expenditure may have to be redirected towards pensions, healthcare and social care at the expense of other essential areas such as education, infrastructure and investment. In countries where population ageing is particularly pronounced, this imbalance can place considerable strain on public finances and on younger generations who are required to support a growing retired population.

In conclusion, older people undoubtedly provide society with valuable experience, knowledge and social contributions, and their role should not be underestimated. However, I believe that the rapid growth of the elderly population creates greater long-term challenges, particularly because of rising healthcare and pension costs and the increasing financial pressure placed on the working-age population. Governments should therefore seek to benefit from the experience of older citizens while simultaneously implementing policies that make ageing societies economically sustainable.
